episode: Josh Radnor discusses _John and Paul_ A Love Story in Song_ with author Ian Leslie

segments.text: As a bonus episode for you this week, we are presenting an interview that Josh conducted with Ian Leslie, author of John and Paul, A Love Story and Song,
a book that Josh and Craig have talked about several times on the podcaSt.
The conversation was originally presented by Barnes & Noble as a live virtual event celebrating the paperback release of the book.
And we've got it here for you right now.
I'm Josh Radner.
I'm delighted to be here.
I'm here with Ian Leslie, the author of John and Paul, A Love Story and Songs, which is a book I just devoured and loved so deeply.
I loved it so much.
I think I was pretty public about my love of the book.
So your people tracked me down knowing that I was a fan to do this.
But welcome.
I'm so delighted to meet you.
Very nice to meet you, Josh.
And it's really lovely to hear.
I'm glad my people tracked you down.
You didn't stand a chance.
Well, I always tell people, let people know when you love something.
You know, it's so nice as a maker of things to get that kind of feedback.
Yes.
And it's also, you know, I think it's nice to talk with people who share an enthusiasm for what you've been writing about.
I will say that I discovered your work because I think like a lot of people, I was it was deep pandemic December 2020, I believe.
And you wrote a post that went pretty viral called 64 Reasons to Celebrate Paul McCartney.
And the starting was after all these years, he's still underrated.
And I know that for me in that moment, like a lot of people, I was hungering for diversion, but also for inspiration to remember there was a big,
beautiful world out there of things to love and appreciate and celebrate.
And this post, and for those listening, if you haven't read this, I just reread it today and it's delightful.
I just I just think it's a wonderful celebration of McCartney.
But I'm curious where the initial impulse to write that post came from.
Were you shocked at its virality, how far it traveled and what role that played in leading to your book, John and Paul, Love Story and Songs?
Yes, great question.
And I'm really pleased that you you came across it.
And that was your kind of route to to the book, because it really that really was the kind of founding moment of John and Paul, a love story and songs.
It's it's not about John and Paul.
It's about Paul.
But it's really kind of it really kind of sparked the book.
Yeah.
Why did I write it?
I mean, like a lot of people, not everyone.
But like a lot of people, I had time on my hands in the in the pandemic.
And I thought, well, I'm going to write this ridiculously long article I kind of have in my head about why Paul McCartney is really good at music.
And I'm not, you know, no magazine is going to buy this, but I've got a substat called The Ruffian and I can publish what the hell I want.
And so I I've been thinking about it and actually writing notes about it for years because I just had this really strong feeling that we don't appreciate what an immense genius Paul McCartney is,
you know, partly because he's still with us.
So we're just like, oh, yeah, it's just Paul McCartney or whatever.
And it's like, no, no, no, guys, this guy is, you know, this is an incredible genius in our midst and we should be grateful and appreciate him.
So I wrote this long post and I yeah, I didn't expect it to many people to read it, apart from a few hardcore kind of fans.
But it went insanely viral and hundreds of thousands of people read it around the world.
And it was also very emotional response.
So people were as you seem to have been right.
People were very touched by it.
And up until then.
The idea of writing a Beatles book hadn't really been on the agenda for me.
I'd written books, you know, but generally my books have been about psychology and, you know, the trait of curiosity.
Or or the conflict and disagreement.
I don't really write about music, but obviously I love music and I've loved the Beatles since I was a kid.
But I didn't really feel licensed to write a book about the Beatles.
And what happened when this post went viral and so many people told me how much they loved it, including some very serious music writers.
I suddenly thought, oh, wow, maybe I could.
Maybe I could write a book about the group that I'd loved since I was a kid.
And the moment I started thinking that, the moment I sort of realized that was a possibility, I thought, well, if I'm going to do that, it's going to be about John and Paul.
I mean, I knew that that was the thing that I really wanted to write a book about.
In fact, when I was writing the Paul McCartney post, I took some of the John and Paul material out because it was already too long.
And I thought, oh, my God, if I get into this, it's going to be another 10,000 words.
So I've got to cut that.
But yeah, so I sort of knew right away that that's the thing I'm most fascinated by, this just inexhaustible fascination of this complex, mysterious,
deep and very moving relationship between these two young men.
Do you feel that because you're not a music writer by trade, was there some liberation in that?
Did you feel that you weren't beholden to certain music journalist tropes that you could just give it your own kind of fans perspective?
Yes, I think that's exactly right.
I think that's exactly right.
I came to it as a bit of an outsider to music journalism, to the tradition of writing about the Beatles, to even to Beatles fandom in a way.
Like, I'm not totally inside the kind of online Beatles world.
I mean, I read a lot of it.
I love it.
But it's not really kind of my thing in particular.
So I'm a sort of partial outsider in more ways than one.
And I think that did really help me kind of write a fresh narrative and a fresh story, because I was always coming to all these stories and narratives and just thinking,
is that really the way I think about it?
And often it wasn't.
So I think that was helpful.
And in a way, it sort of mirrors the relationship of the Beatles to rock and roll, to American music.
You know, they absolutely loved it, but they were also they had this kind of natural distance from it.
And they were kind of looking at it from from a different a different angle.
Right.
Right.
One thing I got very strongly from your article.
Well, when I was reading it, I realized and I never said this out loud, but I was like, oh, I'm a Paul guy.
And I had a roommate in college who was a real John guy.
And he was he was kind of an heir to the tradition.
And you talk about this in both the book and the article that after, you know, post Beatles,
Lennon and Jan Wenner and all these different journalists kind of created this myth around Lennon as the singular genius of the Beatles.
And Paul was this kind of lightweight tunesmith.
And after Lennon died, that myth got even more kind of calcified in the collective conscience.
But it seems to me that your your your work around this stuff, even though the book is really about John and Paul,
it's a bit of a rehabilitation project for Paul on certain in certain ways that that to claim that one was the great genius.
I mean, like they were they had a deeply symbiotic relationship and the Beatles that we love was four, but it was also really two.
And I just love that you kind of balanced the scales on that.
Was that a big was that big in your mind as you were writing the book?
Yes, to some extent.
And I didn't want it to just be, you know, his Paul side of the story, because I wanted to portray what you just described as a deeply symbiotic relationship.
Right.
To show how they each created the other.
And I also wanted to kind of get away from the stereotypes of both in the popular imagination.
But certainly you're right that the one that the person whose reputation has suffered more from this caricature is Paul.
And to some extent, I was kind of making up for that.
But of course, I wasn't the only one.
In fact, you know, you can see his rehabilitation going on in various different ways.
Yeah.
Peter Jackson's get get back movie.
So in a way, I was just part of the general kind of revaluing of Paul.
I think this gone on in the last few years, but I'm definitely proud to be a part of it.
But my other challenge was, you know, my related challenge here was as basically a Paul guy, you know, since I was a kid.
Yeah.
Like, how am I going to bring John Lennon to life sufficiently that a John Lennon fan is is is not going to read this and go, oh, well, he's not very nice to John.
And so I kind of consciously made myself fall in love a bit with John, you know, and that involved talking to people who really love him, who see him as a real, you know,
as he is as a musical genius.
But like, help me understand what made him special, why he's and and just try to look at him from that way as a person and a musician.
And I got there, you know, so in the end, like, I'm still a poor guy, but I love John more than I did before.
And I see them both certainly as more.
Yeah, it's different and more complex than than than cartoons.
One of the delights of reading this book, because you maybe maybe you can describe in broad strokes, like one,
like what this book is and also how you maybe how you kind of pitched it, you know, to publishers.
But one of the delights for me is each section of their, you know, friendship.
And there's a song that goes along where you're showing how their friendships affect the music and the music affect the friendship.
And it's it's really delightful.
I knew most of the songs, but some of them I didn't know.
So so you put the song on either before or after the chapter that you're reading.
And there was there was great joy in that.
But I'm just curious, like how you speak about this book in broad strokes, like how you kind of describe it.
Yeah.
So and yeah, so let's go back to that moment where I was thinking, OK, well, I could I could write a book about the Beatles.
And the thing I'm most interested in is the chemistry between these two young kind of damaged, brilliant young men who meet and essentially just lock into each other.
And it is kind of a love story.
It's almost like love, love at first sight.
And then they go on to have this kind of tender, loving, admiring, but also conflicted and jealousy ridden and sometimes sort of unpleasant, you know, relationship.
But they never really lose that, that they never lose that bond.
Right.
And and the more I thought about it, the more I thought that that kind of is a central thread, you know, maybe even the central thread in the story of the Beatles.
They are kind of a group within a group, these two, you know, even people, even George and Ringo would say, you know, there was us and then there was John and Paul kind of.
And of course, they were the primary songwriters and kind of the most dominant personalities in the group.
And George and Ringo's contributions are immense and indispensable.
I'm not putting, you know, I don't want to marginalize them, but but but absolutely, John and Paul were the kind of engine at the heart of it.
And so I thought, OK, first of all, have there been any books about John and Paul?
Turns out, no, it's like, no, I mean, might have been one or two that I've missed.
But like, in terms of major, significant books, no.
Right.
There's been group biographies of all four of them.
There have been books about the individual Beatles.
And then there were thousands of books about different slices of the story.
But there's no one book about the Leonard McCartney relationship.
Right.
So immediately I thought, well, this is crazy.
And it seemed like an open goal, as we say, in football or soccer.
So I thought, you know, that that encouraged me.
And then I knew pretty much from the beginning that if I was going to tell the story, I would tell it through the songs because.
I don't I don't think you can understand the music of the Beatles without understanding the developing, evolving chemistry of this friendship, this very intense friendship,
this romance, effectively.
And conversely, I don't think you can understand the complexity of that relationship without looking at it through the music, because these guys thought and felt in songs.
Right.
So much of their emotional life was tied up in making songs, in writing songs, in singing with each other.
They weren't particularly emotionally articulate with each other and with others, but they were they were incredibly emotional in their music.
And so I just thought to understand the emotional power of the Beatles, you have to go back to the relationship and to understand the relationship, you have to go to music.
So it's like, well,
I'll just tell the narrative is effectively a biography of the relationship where I start from when they meet in 1957 and I go right through to the end of the friendship,
which is obviously John's death in 1980.
And I tell the whole thing through through the music that they're making and that kind of scheme, that plan for the book kind of came very quickly, which doesn't often happen.
And that was effectively the book that I wrote.
Right.
Were you I mean, it's an amazing thing to find a lane in Beatles scholarship that hasn't been trod.
You know, you know, that you actually found this thing and it was shocking to you that it hadn't been explored.
How much I imagine you there's kind of a trick you would have to do.
I'm making this up as I go.
But this idea of you have all this knowledge of the Beatles in a lifetime of loving the Beatles.
But at the same time, you have to approach it with this kind of beginner's mind.
Yes.
Also excavate.
You're a researcher.
You're a journaliSt.
So I'm curious how you thread the needle between those two things and what shocked and and surprised you as you went that you discovered in addition to, you know,
falling back in love with John.
Yeah.
Great question.
I mean, I don't think I'm not sure that like there was massive shocks and revelations and I didn't expect there to be, you know,
like they're the most sort of studied and covered and filmed and recorded and written about group and people in history.
So the challenge for me was never going to be like, oh, can I turn up some new revelation?
I just I mean, there might be from from other people, but it wasn't something I was going to do.
It's not something I was going to I was not going to go through archives or I didn't do interviews and so on.
It was more like, let's take all the information that's out there and let me find my story, you know, my version of events.
I don't claim to be a scholar laying down the official great story of the Beatles.
I'm like, this is the way I see it, guys.
And and then you're right.
I had to have this kind of beginner's mind where I'm relying on a lot of other sources, effectively.
Well, there's always the primary sources.
You can go to interviews with them.
You can watch them.
You can watch, you know, you can listen to the music.
But there's also lots of secondary sources.
And when I'm reading those secondary sources, I'm thinking,
OK, how much of this do I actually believe?
How much of this story that they're telling do I buy?
And what am I going to bring to it?
Because the last thing I wanted to do was retell the same old stories,
which, frankly, a lot of Beatles journalism and a lot of Beatles authors do, you know, even in part,
even when they're writing something different, part of the book will be, oh, yeah, I know this bit.
I know this bit.
I wanted every page of it to feel fresh in some way.
Yeah.
And and and that meant, yeah, kind of just looking at everything, as you say, with with with fresh eyes.
Yeah, I think there's been I think taking your book along with the Peter Jackson film there,
I think that the Beatles in the popular imagination, you think of like Shea Stadium, you think of Beatlemania.
You there's this kind of like epic, grand, big mythic story that involves fans and critics and 60s and drugs.
And it's just this big, big, big thing.
And what I felt both watching the Peter Jackson documentary and reading your book,
to me, the singular kind of image is them either on LSD or not on LSD, but staring into each other's eyes for as long as they could for hours.
Right.
I mean, just intensely trying to connect.
And it almost feels like you took the macro and you brought it as small as it could go, which is like to their eyeballs.
Yes.
That's beautifully put.
It's beautifully put.
And it was definitely like a central aim of the book was to convey the emotional intimacy of of the relationship.
And I wanted it to be an emotional book.
You know, lots of Beatles books are really fascinating, fun to read, amusing, factually dense.
But there aren't very many of them that really move me.
And that's odd because it's an incredibly moving story.
And the music, of course, is incredibly moving and emotionally powerful because it comes from these emotional guys.
Right.
And so I wanted to kind of, yeah, tell the story in a way that that that touched people and moved people and made them laugh, made them cry,
because that's what the story does does to me.
So, yeah, that's that's right at the heart of it.
Yeah.
And there's a kind of to do that, I think you have to dust off a lot.
You kind of have to demythologize these people.
You have to remove them from the rock Mount Olympus and and really get to the heart of they were teenage boys who'd both lost their mothers,
which is a central kind of psychological.
You know, you go pretty deep into that, that they found each other at this very tender moment in their lives and they saved each other.
I mean, they could have been, you know, fallen into delinquency, but instead they fell into each other.
Sure.
Yeah.
Yeah, that's exactly right.
And, you know,

a lot of the accounts and the way people kind of written have written about or talked about the Beatles and Leonard McCartney specifically were not satisfying to me because they would say things like,
you know,
well, obviously they were great mates or they were like brothers, you know, and I was I was thinking, well, they're nothing like the mates that I have.
You know, I don't have friends like this and I don't like my relationship with my brother is nothing like the relationship.
I have a good relationship with my brother, but it's nothing like John and Paul.
And and then there were some people, you know, there's a minority people of real Beatles, you know, some Beatles fans are like, well,
I think they were secretly homosexual and so on.
I never believed that either.
I felt like people kept trying to put them into these boxes, basically, you know, like, oh, they were friends or they were like brothers.
They were gay, right, because those are the boxes that we have for male relationships.
But there's something about their relationship, their chemistry, which doesn't fit into our usual categories.
And that was kind of skewing the whole thing.
And that's why you end up with these kind of distorted versions of them, because people didn't quite weren't kind of get trying to get to the heart of that.
And that's that's what I was trying to do with the book.
But yeah, there's also a sense of I don't know, the image I'm getting is like an accordion or something where there were moments when they were really far apart.
And then there were moments when they really came together and they they would kind of go back and forth, but they were always dialoguing through the music.
And yeah, they often didn't have the words.
But when they could, I forget, I think Voltaire said that which is too stupid to be said is sung.
You know,
when you get to a point where the sentiment is too big and it would it would shrivel with words that you almost need a melody to carry the truth or the sentiment of what you're trying to express.
And it felt to me that they were music was the only way they could truly communicate, both because of, you know, male bravado or the time and place.
I mean, it really is a study in they gave it their all like in the healthiest way they knew how and maybe I bet they they'd be much more if they were brought up today,
they might be much more emotionally expressive.
Yeah, we might not have we wouldn't have had the Beatles.
Yeah, I mean, it's the whole story is a great testament to the sheer power of emotional male repression.
And, you know, it's like, yeah, I mean, it's partly just because they're men, it's partly because they were growing up in the 1950s.
You know, there's that heartbreaking quote that I use from from early and Paul, you know, when after Paul's mother dies and his auntie Jin, whom he loved, who was a lovely auntie,
said, you know, you got to pull yourself together, essentially.
And, you know, she says to him and to Paul and Mike, well, listen, boys, you know, your mother's dead.
And that's that's sad.
But like, you got to look after your dad now.
OK, that's it.
That was the amount of therapy that he had or whatever, like that was the amount of people kind of listening was saying, well, how are you feeling?
Let's talk through it and so on.
They didn't get that.
They were just like, OK, let's get on with it, guys.
And that was the way he did things.
You know, if you'd grown up in poverty, as his parents and his aunts had, or if you'd been through war, as they had, you had to keep going.
But but it meant that obviously all his hurt and pain and confusion was kind of like sealed up and locked away.
And and John, I mean, we don't have time to go through this, the kind of disruptive, like disruptiveness and the pain and confusion of his childhood.
But but but obviously, like he had a lot to deal with and he wouldn't have had sufficient outlet for either.
And so, yeah, what do you do with all these emotions that are swirling around and all these questions?
You don't really get to talk about them very much.
So you pour them into this incredibly intense music that you that you've fallen in love with.
And that's that's how they learn that their relationship with with music was as a place like, you know, I was listening to somebody talk about Shakespeare's sonnets,
which are very kind of a lot of them are very emotionally intense.
And they seem to be about kind of love affairs that he was having.
And of course, they have this very precise form.
I can't remember what it is, like 14 lines and a couple at the end.
But and the the the the the critic said, you know, so basically there were like an emotional panic room for Shakespeare.
He could put all these emotions into this like for and the pop song was like that for John and Paul.
Right.
You know, it had a form.
It had a, you know, verse chorus two minutes long and it's got to have a hook and so on.
So whatever you where whatever your feelings are, you can go, OK, I've got to make something out of this.
Of course, if you go into therapy, the first thing they say is like, we're going to take this big mess of emotion.
We're going to put some structure around it and that's going to help you process it.
So basically pop music, rock and roll music becomes a way for them to process these otherwise overwhelming emotions.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I am.
I it seems that when people die, it's easier in some ways to get a handle on who they were and what they were about.
And there's something lovely about eulogizing the living.
I remember we honored an acting teacher at NYU when he was retiring and he said it's so nice to not have to die to get this kind of feedback, you know,
that he got to be there to hear it.
And I've often thought about I love another songwriter I adore is Jackson Brown.
And I've often thought if Jackson Brown died at 27 and he had those first three out, you know, he'd be this absolute, you know, Mount Rushmore kind of songwriter.
But I think that, you know, there was something about being able to celebrate.
It just occurs to me that Paul got twice the life that John did.
And in some ways it makes how, you know, the mind is you just do all these kind of thought experiments around what could have happened if that hadn't happened.
But like, I don't know, I don't know if there's a question attached to this, but it but it just occurred to me that it's a lot easier to in some ways, yeah,
to eulogize the dead rather than eulogize the living.
But I'm glad that Paul is around for some of this celebration.
Yeah.
And I mean, it also makes you reflect on how young John Lennon was when he died.
And, you know, it felt like at the time, like he was old, he's middle-aged, I suppose.
I suppose he's officially middle-aged, but like, especially as one gets older and you pass the age of 40 and you go like, yeah, but that was young.
That was really young.
And I kind of feel like, you know, he didn't get a chance to really, in a sense, because he was such a difficult, you know, character.
There was a lot more development to go.
I mean, do you know what I mean?
Like, emotional and personal and artistic, I'm sure, you know, there was a long road ahead.
So it's very sad.
And of course, it was very, very sad for Paul.
And I think Paul, at different levels and in different ways, has missed him, you know, for the last 40 years.
I think he still misses him.
That, you know, even though he found him difficult and annoying and all sorts of things, frustrating, I think he was always his cellmate and he was bound to miss his cellmate.
Yeah.
Yeah, there's some beautiful stuff in the book about how post-Beatles, I think Paul even is asked, you know, what he plans to do.
And he says, I intend to grow up, you know, that there that there seemed to be Lennon seemed to have a bigger Peter Pan kind of thing going than McCartney did, who said, like, no,
I'm going to be with this woman.
I'm going to raise this stepkid.
I'm going to have kids.
I'm going to live in the country.
And, yeah, it was just that's that's another fascinating thing you follow is when the Beatles split up the book.
There's quite a bit more book left after the Beatles split up, you know, that they were still in each other, not being in the band.
I mean, in a way, it's one of the most fascinating periods because they know they really can only talk to each other through songs.
I mean, they still after they they fall out, then they kind of make up, you know, in the early 70s.
And so they are in touch throughout most of the 70s and they're talking on the phone and then and they're visiting each other's families now and again.
But they can't recover that old intimacy because they're not face to face and they're not making music.
Right.
And the relationship was always about being face to face and making music.
And so what do they do?
They start, you know, even more than they were doing in the 60s, because I think they did it all the way through.
But they start kind of writing songs, you know, with messages to each other.
Yeah.
You know, how do you sleep is a nasty one from John that he writes.
And but then, you know, he seemed to say at some point that the jealous guy was was a kind of a reconciliatory song.
And partly about Paul, you know, you're on Paul's side.
You've got songs like Let Me Roll It.
And so that dialogue went on at a distance through the 70s.
And there's a real beauty and sort of poignancy about that.
Yeah.
They also they also see and we're going to move on to audience questions in a moment.
But it also seems they spurred each other on to greatness because they had this deep desire to impress the other person.
They were the only opinions that truly mattered.
Yeah.
Other.
And in that weird combustion, we got all this great music and now we have this great book.
I think that's right.
The competitiveness.
That was the other thing.
People always thought about, oh, they're really competitive and they hated each other by about 1965 or whatever.
I mean, that was nonsense.
I mean, they were competitive, but but they were all they were collaborating all the way through the 60s and and they always admired each other.
They always.
And so, yeah, they were competitive, but in the sense that they were delighted when the other one outdid them because it meant that they would have to do something even greater.
Yeah.
So, John, you know, Paul, his strawberry fields forever.
And he's like, oh, my God, that's incredible.
What am I going to do?
Yeah.
Penny Lane.
And I think John was delighted by that.
Right.
That that that's the kind of creative, loving, productive competition that they had.
So here are a couple of audience questions.
Can you talk?
I mean, you talk briefly that you didn't.
You didn't.
Did you talk to anyone in the estates of these people or just some of your research methods and your routines for writing the book?
No, I didn't.
I was toying with the idea of interviews at the beginning, and I did interview Michael Lindsay Hogg, who was very gracious and very, very interesting.
But I quickly decided I don't think this is going to be interviews.
I mean, basically, all the people that were around them and including, you know, Paul and Ringo, it was a long time ago that their memories are not great.
And so what they do is they repeat the story that they last told.
And so what you've got is just like stories building on stories, building on stories.
And and the problem with that is, A, they're not very reliable.
And B, we've heard them all before.
Yeah.
And so I thought it's actually more valuable to just go through the archive and go through everything that's the published record that's out there and go, like,
look at the interviews from 1966 or 1968 and 1973.
Like, what's what are they saying at the time, as well as what they're saying later?
Yeah.
And just pull it all together.
You don't actually need to go and do try and get interviews with people who will just tell you the same story they told, you know, the New York Post or whatever.
Right.
Right.
Someone just asked, after writing this book, do you have a new favorite song?
Oh, good question.
I think it.
God, yeah, I have new favorite songs all the time.
But but maybe it gave me an even deeper and richer appreciation of the songs from the kind of last year of their life,
because they're so now they're so deep and layered with the emotions of the group.
And the relationship coming apart, you know, and kind of waving goodbye to it.
So, you know, if I had to name one, I'd say you never give me your money, which I just think is just emotionally devastating.
And and and and and part of the reason I should never say is that they're playing so well together.
Like it's an incredible ensemble piece.
It's like they're all contributing, but it's essentially a song about them splitting up.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And also, I mean, just seeing those rooftop performances, you're like, I mean, one, they I think they look the coolest of any human ever.
But yeah, but the way that they are so effortlessly in sync and at ease with each other and right before the end to I read a New Yorker article on McCartney that I loved years ago.
So and he I think did you see Man on the Run, the doc?
Yes.
Yeah.
I quite enjoyed that, too, about his post Beatles years with the wings with wings.
And and you were a wings guy, too, right?
Oh, yeah.
I love wings.
Yeah.
But he has a it my sense was the combination of the the fallout over the band, but not just the band.
There was a lot of and you go into this with the managers and Apple, you know, the the business and the rupture.
It was it was almost more of a business rupture than a creative rupture in some ways.
